query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high-entropy alloys, a higher concentration of reactive elements (e.g., Cr and/or Al) drives their preferential segregation to the surface during high-temperature exposure, which in turn enables the rapid nucleation and continuous self-healing of a thin, adherent protective oxide layer.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, single-phase HEA (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi) with a baseline lower reactive element (Cr/Al) concentration.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the concentration of key reactive elements (such as Cr and/or Al) in the HEA while keeping the remaining composition constant.
generation.conditions: Expose the samples to an oxidizing environment at elevated temperatures (800–1200 °C) under controlled atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a surface-enriched region in the alloy, where increased levels of reactive elements accumulate at the oxide/alloy interface.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, the sluggish diffusion in the multi-element matrix combined with the concentration gradient promotes selective segregation of Cr/Al to the surface. These enriched reactive elements then enable a rapid nucleation and growth of a compact, self-healing oxide scale that acts as a diffusion barrier against further oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline HEA with lower reactive element content, alloys with increased Cr/Al concentrations will form a thinner, more uniform, and adherent oxide layer with slower overall mass gain. In-situ surface analysis should reveal significant enrichment of these elements at the interface during oxidation.
generation.baseline: HEA alloys with a lower concentration of reactive elements, which are expected to form thicker, less uniform oxide layers with more defects and faster oxidation kinetics.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to single-phase HEAs exposed to high-temperature oxidizing conditions (800–1200 °C). Its applicability to multiphase alloys or different temperature/atmosphere regimes remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold of reactive element concentration required to trigger effective surface segregation and the quantitative relationship between segregation kinetics and oxide protection remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of otherwise identical single-phase HEAs with systematically varied reactive element (Cr/Al) concentrations. Expose these samples to controlled high-temperature oxidizing conditions (800–1200 °C). Use in-situ high-temperature surface characterization techniques (such as XPS or TEM) to monitor surface elemental segregation, and perform thermogravimetric analysis along with microscopy (SEM/TEM) to measure oxide layer thickness, uniformity, and growth kinetics.
measurements: Surface elemental concentration profiles (using XPS or SIMS)
Oxide layer thickness and morphology (using SEM/TEM)
Oxidation kinetics via mass gain (using thermogravimetric analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If altering the reactive element concentration does not lead to significant differences in the surface enrichment, oxide scale uniformity, or oxidation kinetics—i.e., if all samples, regardless of reactive element levels, exhibit similar oxide morphology and growth rates—then the hypothesis that reactive-element segregation governs the formation and retention of a protective oxide layer is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. First reported in 2004 [ [1] ], high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys comprising five or more elements in equal or nearly equal molar fractions, with each element present at a mole fraction of approximately 5–35 at.% [ [2] ]. The presence of multiple elements leads to a high configurational entropy, resulting in solid-solution structures with face-centred cubic (FCC) and body-centred cubic (BCC) lattices, rather than intermetallic compounds [ [3] ]. In recent years, HEAs have garnered significant consideration in the field of materials science because of their exceptional performance characteristics, including high strength [ [4] ], corrosion resistance [ [5] ], soft magnetic properties [ [6] ], high hardness [ [7] ], wear resistance [ [8] ], fatigue resistance [ [9] ], and softening resistance at high temperatures [ [10] ]. The superior high-temperature behaviour of HEAs can be attributed to four underlying effects: the high entropy effect, the sluggish kinetic diffusion effect, the severe lattice distortion effect, and the cocktail effect [ [11] ].

Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides. frame.system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) designed as single-phase, multicomponent solid solutions for high-temperature applications, initially in a homogenized state prior to oxidation.
frame.goal: To mechanistically explain how these HEAs develop and sustain a protective oxide layer that imparts oxidation resistance at elevated temperatures.
frame.limitation: The precise mechanism responsible for the formation and retention of a protective, self-healing oxide scale in HEAs remains unverified, particularly regarding the role of elemental segregation and diffusion kinetics relative to simpler alloys.
root_cause_cues: develop and retain a protective oxide layer
constraints: Must specify the governing mechanism (i.e., what elemental interactions or diffusion processes lead to protective oxide formation and retention)
Needs a controlled comparison (e.g., varying the concentration of key reactive elements or comparing with non-HEA alloys)
Should outline expected observations relative to a baseline alloy (e.g., differences in oxide scale thickness, uniformity, and adherence)
Applicable boundaries (e.g., temperature range, oxidizing atmosphere conditions)
Must be supported by prior evidence from oxidation or diffusion studies in HEAs/related systems
The hypothesis must incorporate a clear, falsifiable prediction.
frame.regime: High-temperature oxidizing environments (e.g., 800–1200 °C) where diffusion kinetics and oxide scale formation are critical.
prior_attempts: Comparative studies showing that HEAs with reactive elements (such as Cr, Al, or Si) exhibit slower oxidation rates compared to conventional alloys, but without a unified, testable mechanistic explanation linking elemental segregation/diffusion to oxide scale stability.
Investigations into single-phase vs. multiphase alloys that noted differences in oxidation behavior, yet lacked controlled comparisons directly testing the role of internal elemental redistribution.
frame.understanding: The hypothesis posits that in high-entropy alloys, the complex multicomponent environment drives preferential surface segregation of reactive elements (e.g., Al, Cr). This segregation creates a locally enriched region at the alloy surface that promotes the rapid nucleation and growth of a dense, adherent oxide layer. The multielement nature of HEAs offers a self-healing mechanism due to continuous diffusion of reactive elements from the bulk to the surface, thereby replenishing the protective scale and maintaining oxidation resistance under high-temperature conditions. A controlled experiment comparing HEAs with deliberately varied concentrations of these reactive elements (versus baseline alloys lacking such concentration gradients) should reveal that only alloys that exhibit significant element segregation form a uniform, slow-growing oxide film. Observations would include a thinner, more continuous, and adherent oxide layer with fewer defects relative to the control. A result showing no difference in oxide morphology or growth kinetics when reactive element concentrations are altered (or if competing diffusion pathways do not result in surface enrichment) would falsify the hypothesis.

decision.trend: Earlier investigations in high-entropy alloys focused first on observing that alloy chemistry and processing-induced microstructural changes (e.g., ultrafine grain sizes) significantly influence oxidation behavior. Studies demonstrated that HEAs with refined grain structures tend to form thinner, more uniform oxides (as seen with the ultrafine-grained AlCoCrFeNi alloys) and that reactive elements like Cr can modify the oxide phase (evidenced by Cr-content variations in refractory coatings). In these works, modifying either the processing route (e.g., friction processing) or the reactive element concentration led to changes in diffusion pathways and oxide scale characteristics. However, while there is ample evidence that reactive-element segregation and diffusion contribute to forming a protective oxide layer, a direct testable link that quantitatively correlates segregation kinetics with oxide scale self-healing and long-term protection remains unestablished.
decision.unsolved: A clear, mechanistic, and falsifiable hypothesis remains to be proven that directly ties the kinetics of reactive-element (e.g., Cr or Al) segregation/diffusion to the formation, uniformity, and self-healing behavior of the protective oxide layer in single-phase HEAs under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the concentration of key reactive elements (such as Cr and/or Al) in an otherwise identical single-phase HEA, then monitor the real-time evolution of surface oxide scales (using in-situ high-temperature characterization techniques like XPS or TEM coupled with thermogravimetric analysis) over the 800–1200 °C range.
decision.why: This approach builds on prior evidence that both microstructure and reactive element content influence oxidation kinetics. By isolating the effect of the reactive element concentration on the diffusion-driven segregation process at the oxide/alloy interface, the experiment directly tests the hypothesis that enhanced surface enrichment from the bulk leads to a denser, self-healing oxide. Failure to observe significant differences in oxide morphology or kinetics when reactive element levels are altered would directly falsify the hypothesis.
